title: How does work survive failures?
summary: Follow one accepted video through durable state, duplicate messages, worker leases and safe retries.
opening_answer: Requests repeat, messages arrive twice and workers die. SQL holds authoritative state; outbox and inbox rows bridge the queue; source versions pin exact bytes; attempt leases stop an old worker completing newer work.

sections.title: An asset, a job and an attempt are different things

blocks.text: Asset: the owner's video. Job: the work requested. Attempt: one try. Retry means same source, new attempt.

rows: Who owns what, and which bytes were accepted.

Requested work, each execution, repeated retry requests.
Received messages and durable send intentions.

blocks.text: Job states: queued, processing, done, failed, cancelled; attempts can also be abandoned or succeeded. A failed job returns to queued via a new attempt from a legitimate retry, not queue redelivery.

blocks.q: What is the difference between retrying a job and receiving a duplicate message?
blocks.a: A retry creates a new attempt for accepted work. A duplicate message repeats the same transport instruction and must not create a second logical operation.

sections.title: Uploading bytes is not yet accepting work

steps.label: Reserve
steps.detail: Owner-scoped reservation (size, hash, type, expiry, server-chosen S3 key) and a constrained presigned POST.

steps.label: Send bytes
steps.detail: Straight to S3; the API never proxies the video.

steps.label: Finalize
steps.detail: Media verifies the object, pins its S3 VersionId, then commits asset and outbox intent together.

blocks.text: Reservations expire after 15 minutes; source limit 100 MiB. Finalization checks the stored object, not the client's claim. The hash names expected bytes; the VersionId names the exact object, so overwriting the key cannot change an accepted source.
Missing object: recoverable 409, nothing adopted. Storage outage: 503 (wait). Expired reservation: 410 (reserve anew).

blocks.q: Why pin a VersionId when the object already has a key?
blocks.a: A key names a location whose contents can change; the version pin selects the exact accepted bytes.

sections.title: The failure between saving and sending

blocks.text: Crash after saving but before sending to SQS leaves an accepted asset with no work. Sending first risks queued work for a rolled-back transaction.

spec.title: Make the intention durable first

steps.label: One transaction
steps.detail: Business change and message intent commit together, or neither does.

steps.label: Publish later
steps.detail: A publisher claims a due row and sends outside the lock; lost replies can cause a re-send.

steps.label: Accept once
steps.detail: Consumer checks message identity, updates state and stages follow-ups before acknowledging.

spec.caption: Closes the lost-intent gap; not one transaction across two databases and SQS, not exactly-once.

blocks.text: Inbox stores message ID and body hash: same ID and content is recognized; same ID with different content is a conflict. A claim token stops an obsolete publisher overwriting a later outcome; row locks and uniqueness constraints enforce it.

blocks.q: Why is an outbox needed if SQS is already durable?
blocks.a: SQS preserves a message once it has it. The outbox covers the earlier gap between committing state and sending.
No. Transport is at-least-once. Inbox checks, idempotent transitions and worker fences aim at one correct logical result despite duplicates.

sections.title: Why a worker needs a lease

blocks.text: Starting a container is not permission to finish a job. A worker claims the current attempt and a time-limited lease token; heartbeats extend it. Database clock, attempt and token decide whether a finish is valid.
If worker A stalls, recovery retires its attempt; when A wakes, a fence checks it still owns the attempt and lease. Attempt-specific output paths prevent overwrites.

blocks.q: Why is a queue visibility timeout not enough to protect completion?
blocks.a: Visibility controls delivery, not ownership of job state; a worker can outlive its message’s invisibility. The SQL attempt and lease fence decides if it may complete.

sections.title: A repeated click is an identity problem

blocks.text: A timeout does not say whether the server committed. Publisher keeps a stable intent key per uncertain mutation, scoped to API base and owner; repeats reuse identity and content. After confirmed acceptance, publishing again is a new intention. Not directory sync or global deduplication.

Media stores request identities and fingerprints; a reused key with different content is rejected. Finalization rechecks the row under a lock after verification, so simultaneous requests cannot both adopt it; the slow object check runs outside locks.

blocks.language: Illustrative pseudocode — the actual code is linked below
blocks.text:
verify_the_object_without_holding_a_row_lock()
with owner_database_transaction():
    reservation = lock_and_reload_reservation()
    if already_finalized:
        return_existing_asset()
    pin_verified_version()
    save_asset()
    stage_processing_command()
# The outbox publisher sends after this transaction commits.

blocks.q: Why not generate a fresh request key after every timeout?
blocks.a: The earlier request may have committed; a fresh key is a new intention and may duplicate work. Reusing identity lets the server recognize the replay.

sections.title: Deletion and repair are workflows too

blocks.text: Deletion spans SQL and object storage: record a tombstone or cleanup intent, hide the content, retry object cleanup. Late results cannot revive a deleted asset; a submission guard handles cancel-before-submit.

Repair must be bounded: endless rereads of old reservations keep an idle database awake. The fix backs off rescans and retires clean records after the horizon; failed scans are not declared finished. At the earlier freeze Aurora read zero capacity about 56 minutes after the last upload (point-in-time, not a bill). Each service now has its own cluster (AD-29).
Limits: no demonstrated restore drill, no general retention deadline for active media. Reliability means explicit invariants and bounded repair.

blocks.q: Why not immediately remove every database row when an owner deletes a video?
blocks.a: State must survive to reject late messages, remember cancellation and finish cleanup. Hiding the resource and recording intent beats forgetting early.

takeaways: Distinguish asset, job, attempt and lease.
Explain the save-then-send gap and the outbox.
Duplicates are expected; stale workers are fenced.
Retrying one request differs from a new intention.
